title: Third commandment (CCC 2168–2195)
hookLine: Sunday rest, worship and time for family and the poor

cards: Sunday, 9:14 p.m. An email lands with the subject line: quick question. It isn't quick, and it isn't really a question.

The laptop opens, and the evening is gone. Somewhere else, a family has had pancakes, gone to Mass, visited an aunt in a nursing home, and is now arguing cheerfully over a board game. Both are Sundays.
Only one looks different from the other six days. This is the commandment that sets a day apart.

teach.h: GOD RESTED ON THE SEVENTH DAY.
teach.b: You met Sunday in your first weeks and the Sabbath in year one. In the Douay-Rheims: "Remember that thou keep holy the sabbath day." The Catechism roots it in creation: God worked six days and rested on the seventh.
Rest isn't laziness; it's something God himself is pictured doing.
In Jewish tradition, the Sabbath is the seventh day, and the Catechism honors it as a sign of the covenant and a day of freedom, when even servants and animals rest.
Jesus keeps the Sabbath, and in Mark he says: "Therefore the Son of man is Lord of the sabbath also."

teach.h: THE LORD'S DAY: MASS AND REST.
teach.b: Christians came to gather on the first day of the week, the day of the resurrection, the Lord's Day.

The Catechism quotes Justin Martyr, an early Christian writer, on believers gathering on the day of the sun; in the same passage, Justin describes people from town and country meeting on Sunday to hear the apostles' writings and share the Eucharist.
So the Catholic Sunday has two sides. Worship: Catholics are obliged to take part in Mass on Sundays and holy days, unless excused for a serious reason like illness or the care of infants.
And rest: avoiding work or business that gets in the way of worship, joy, works of mercy and the relaxation of mind and body.

teach.h: TIME FOR FAMILY AND THE POOR.
teach.b: Then the circle widens: time for family, often scattered during the week; for the sick and the elderly; for silence and study.
And a line for employers and every Christian: don't make needless demands that keep others from keeping the Lord's Day. Rest, here, isn't only for you.

how: Catholics keep Sunday, or a Saturday evening vigil Mass, by going to Mass and resting from unneeded work; families may set aside the day for a shared meal, visits and time together.

games.q: the third commandment — tap the pairs.
p: the first day of the week
gathering on the day called Sunday
the Son of man, Lord of the sabbath also

s: Catholics may never work at all on Sunday
the Catechism allows for family needs and important service; what it asks is to avoid work that gets in the way of worship and rest.
the Catechism says Sunday is time for the sick and the elderly
it names family, the sick, the infirm and the elderly, and works of mercy.
Sunday rest is only about the person resting
the Catechism asks people not to make needless demands that keep others from keeping the day.

games.q: it's Sunday, and you run a small shop. you could ask your one employee to come in for a few extra hours of sorting stock that could easily wait. what does the Catechism ask?
o: call her in; work is work.
avoid needless demands that keep others from the Lord's Day.
games.why: the Catechism asks Christians not to make needless demands that would keep others from keeping Sunday.

practice: Look ahead to the coming Sunday and choose one thing to set down, the inbox, the errand that can wait, and one thing to put in its place: an unhurried meal, a walk, a visit to someone who's alone.
If you go to Mass, picture arriving unhurried. If you pray, offer the day to God now, in advance; if not, just let the plan sit for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Third commandment. Remember that thou keep holy the sabbath day: for Catholics, Sunday, the Lord's Day, kept with Mass, rest, family, and care for the poor and sick. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Sabbath, the day of rest.

carryVoice: Your line: keep holy the day. One day in seven can look different from the rest. Rest well.
